def: A secret word or code you type to enter a system or account.
ex: You should change your password every few months to keep your account safe.
nat: I forgot my password, so I asked the system to send me a reset link.

mis.bad: Please digit your password.
mis.good: Please type your password.
mis.why: "Digitar" is "type" in English; "digit" only means a number character like 5.

def: To copy a file from the internet to your own device.
ex: I downloaded the report to my laptop so I could read it on the train.
nat: You can download the app for free from the official website.

mis.bad: I did the download of the file yesterday.
mis.good: I downloaded the file yesterday.
mis.why: Use download as a verb (downloaded) instead of "do the download of".

def: To send a file from your device to the internet or another system.
ex: She uploaded the photos to the shared folder before the meeting started.
nat: It took ages to upload the video because the connection was so slow.

mis.bad: I uploaded the file in the cloud.
mis.good: I uploaded the file to the cloud.
mis.why: Use "to" with upload, not "in", when you send a file to a place.

def: To put a program on a computer so that it is ready to use.
ex: I installed the new software yesterday, but it still doesn't open properly.
nat: You need to install the latest version before you can join the call.

mis.bad: I need to instal the program.
mis.good: I need to install the program.
mis.why: In English the verb is spelled with two l's: install.

def: Programs and instructions that make a computer do tasks.
ex: Our company buys software from several suppliers to manage its customer data.
nat: This software is easy to learn, even for people with no experience.

mis.bad: I bought two softwares for the office.
mis.good: I bought two pieces of software for the office.
mis.why: Software is uncountable, so it has no plural; say "a piece of software".

def: A group of computers or devices that are connected to share information.
ex: The whole office lost internet access because of a problem with the network.
nat: Please connect to the guest network if you are visiting our office.

mis.bad: I connected in the network.
mis.good: I connected to the network.
mis.why: Connect takes "to".

def: A powerful computer that stores data and provides services to other computers.
ex: The website went down for an hour because the server ran out of memory.
nat: We moved all our files to a new server last weekend.

mis.bad: The servant is not responding.
mis.good: The server is not responding.
mis.why: "Servant" means a person who serves; for a computer, use server.

def: A set of connected pages on the internet with one address.
ex: Our website gets about ten thousand visitors every day, mostly from mobile phones.
nat: I couldn't find the price on their website, so I called the shop.

mis.bad: I saw it in the site of the company.
mis.good: I saw it on the company's website.
mis.why: Use "on" for websites, not "in": on the website.

def: A program you use to look at pages on the internet.
ex: If the page looks strange, try opening it in a different browser.
nat: I cleared the cache in my browser, and then the site loaded normally.

mis.bad: I opened the navigator and searched for it.
mis.good: I opened the browser and searched for it.
mis.why: "Navegador" is "browser" in English; "navigator" is not used for this.

def: A computer program designed to do a particular job, often called an app.
ex: This application helps small teams plan their projects and share files easily.
nat: She developed a mobile application that tracks how much water you drink.

mis.bad: She works with application development of mobile.
mis.good: She works in mobile application development.
mis.why: Put the modifier first: "mobile application development".

def: A useful part or function of a product or program.
ex: The new camera has a feature that automatically blurs the background of photos.
nat: One feature I really like is the dark mode at night.

mis.bad: This phone has many functionalities.
mis.good: This phone has many features.
mis.why: "Functionalities" is rarely used; say "features" for what a product can do.

def: A mistake in a program that makes it work incorrectly.
ex: The developers are working to fix a bug that deletes saved settings.
nat: We found a serious bug just before the product launch.

mis.bad: The program has a lot of erros.
mis.good: The program has a lot of bugs.
mis.why: In software, a mistake in the code is a bug, not an "error" in everyday speech about problems.

def: Instructions written in a programming language for a computer.
ex: He spent the whole afternoon reading old code to understand how the system works.
nat: Please add comments to your code so other people can understand it.

mis.bad: I am learning to code in Python language.
mis.good: I am learning to code in Python.
mis.why: Say "in Python"; adding the word "language" is unnecessary and sounds strange.

def: Unwanted messages, usually advertising, sent to many people by email.
ex: Most of the emails I get every morning are spam, so I delete them quickly.
nat: My email filter catches almost all the spam before I see it.

mis.bad: I received many spams today.
mis.good: I received a lot of spam today.
mis.why: Spam is uncountable, so it never takes an -s.

def: A personal record with your details that lets you use a service.
ex: You need to create an account before you can buy anything on this site.
nat: She logged in to her account and changed her email address.

mis.bad: I opened an account in the website.
mis.good: I opened an account on the website.
mis.why: Use "on" with websites.

def: Options on a device or program that you can change.
ex: You can turn off notifications in the settings of your phone.
nat: I changed the privacy settings so only my friends can see my photos.

mis.bad: I entered in the configurations of the phone.
mis.good: I opened the settings on the phone.
mis.why: In apps and devices, "configurações" is usually "settings", not "configurations".

def: A device that stores power so a phone or laptop can work without a cable.
ex: My phone battery only lasts half a day now, so I carry a charger.
nat: The battery died during the meeting, and I could not find a socket.

mis.bad: My battery is discharged.
mis.good: My battery is dead.
mis.why: Use "dead" or "flat" for an empty battery; "discharged" is unnatural.

def: Not using cables or wires to connect to a network or device.
ex: We bought wireless headphones so we can walk around while we talk.
nat: The wireless signal is weak in the back room of the house.

mis.bad: I prefer the wireless of the hotel.
mis.good: I prefer the hotel's wireless internet.
mis.why: Wireless is an adjective, so it needs a noun after it, like wireless internet.

def: A link between a device and a network, or between two things.
ex: I lost my connection during the video call, so I had to rejoin.
nat: A stable connection is essential if you want to work from home.

mis.bad: My conection is very bad.
mis.good: My connection is very bad.
mis.why: The spelling is connection with "ct", not "c" like in Portuguese "conexão".

def: A wave that carries information such as a phone call or internet data.
ex: I can't call you from here because there is no signal in the basement.
nat: The phone shows a strong signal, but the internet is still slow.

mis.bad: I have no sign in my phone.
mis.good: I have no signal on my phone.
mis.why: Use signal for phone or wifi reception; "sign" means a symbol or notice.

def: To remove a file, message, or other data from a device.
ex: I accidentally deleted the folder that contained all my photos from the trip.
nat: Please delete the old emails to free up some space.

mis.bad: I deleted my account of the website.
mis.good: I deleted my account on the website.
mis.why: Use "on" with websites and services, not "of".

def: A collection of data stored on a computer under one name.
ex: The file was too large to send by email, so I shared a link.
nat: Save the file on your desktop so you can find it easily.

mis.bad: I saved the archive on my desktop.
mis.good: I saved the file on my desktop.
mis.why: "Archive" is a compressed or stored collection; for a normal computer file, say file.

def: A place on a computer where you keep a group of files together.
ex: I created a separate folder for each client to keep everything organized.
nat: Can you move these documents into the shared folder, please?

mis.bad: I put the files inside the folder of the desktop.
mis.good: I put the files in a folder on the desktop.
mis.why: Use "in a folder" and "on the desktop", not "inside the folder of".

def: A file that you send together with an email message.
ex: I forgot the attachment, so I had to send a second email.
nat: Don't open an attachment if you don't know who sent it.

mis.bad: I am sending the annex with the file.
mis.good: I am sending the file as an attachment.
mis.why: "Annex" is not used for emails; the file you attach is an attachment.

def: The place in an email program where new messages arrive.
ex: My inbox is full of messages I haven't had time to answer.
nat: She checks her inbox first thing every morning before she starts work.

mis.bad: I have 300 e-mails not read in my inbox.
mis.good: I have 300 unread emails in my inbox.
mis.why: Use the adjective "unread" before the noun.

def: The flat surface of a device where you see pictures and text.
ex: Looking at a screen for too long gives me a headache.
nat: The screen on my phone cracked when I dropped it on the floor.

mis.bad: I looked the screen all day.
mis.good: I looked at the screen all day.
mis.why: Look needs "at" before the thing you are watching.

def: A set of keys that you press to type letters and numbers.
ex: I spilled coffee on my keyboard, and now some of the keys don't work.
nat: You can use the keyboard shortcut Control and C to copy the text.

mis.bad: I pressed the button Enter on the keyboard.
mis.good: I pressed the Enter key on the keyboard.
mis.why: Keys on a keyboard are called "keys", and the key name comes before it.

def: A thick wire used to carry electricity or data between devices.
ex: I need a longer cable to connect my laptop to the big monitor.
nat: The cable was damaged, so the phone would not charge.

mis.bad: I need a cable to connect the computer in the monitor.
mis.good: I need a cable to connect the computer to the monitor.
mis.why: Connect takes "to" before the second item.

def: A website where a person regularly writes about a topic.
ex: She writes a blog about traveling alone and saving money.
nat: I found the answer on a blog written by an experienced engineer.

mis.bad: I wrote a post in my blog yesterday.
mis.good: I wrote a post on my blog yesterday.
mis.why: Use "on" with blogs and websites, not "in".

def: A message, picture, or text that someone publishes online.
ex: Her post about the new phone got thousands of likes in one day.
nat: I read your post about learning English, and I found it very helpful.

mis.bad: I did a post on the Instagram.
mis.good: I made a post on Instagram.
mis.why: Use "make a post" or "write a post"; "do a post" is not natural, and no "the" before Instagram.

def: A written opinion or remark that someone adds below a post or document.
ex: Someone left a rude comment under my video, so I deleted it.
nat: Please read the comments in the document before you edit it.

mis.bad: I made a comment in the video of the channel.
mis.good: I left a comment on the channel's video.
mis.why: Say "leave a comment on" a video; "in the video of the channel" is unnatural.

def: To let other people see or use something that you have.
ex: He shared the link with everyone in the team so they could join.
nat: You can share your screen during the call if you want to show the results.

mis.bad: I shared the file to my colleagues.
mis.good: I shared the file with my colleagues.
mis.why: Use "with" for the people you share something with, not "to".

def: Connected to the internet or available on the internet.
ex: More and more people prefer to do their shopping online instead of going to stores.
nat: She takes an online course in data analysis on weekends.

mis.bad: I am on-line since morning.
mis.good: I have been online since this morning.
mis.why: Use the present perfect "have been online since" with a time point, and write online as one word.

def: Not connected to the internet or to a network.
ex: The app works offline, so you can use it on a plane.
nat: The server was offline for two hours during the maintenance.

mis.bad: I am off-line now.
mis.good: I am offline now.
mis.why: The word is written as one word: offline.

def: Using computers and electronic technology to store or send information.
ex: Many banks now offer digital services, so fewer people visit the branches.
nat: She prefers reading digital books because she can carry hundreds of them.

mis.bad: I prefer digital books than paper books.
mis.good: I prefer digital books to paper books.
mis.why: Prefer uses "to", not "than".

def: A machine that can do tasks automatically, sometimes like a human.
ex: The factory uses a robot to move heavy boxes from one area to another.
nat: Robots can work all day without getting tired.

mis.bad: Robots will substitute many workers.
mis.good: Robots will replace many workers.
mis.why: "Substituir" is usually "replace"; "substitute" is not used with a direct object like this.

def: Existing on a computer or online instead of in the physical world.
ex: We held a virtual meeting because half of the team was abroad.
nat: You can take a virtual tour of the museum from home.

mis.bad: The reunion will be virtual.
mis.good: The meeting will be virtual.
mis.why: "Reunion" is a meeting of people who have not seen each other for a long time; Portuguese "reunião" is "meeting".

def: A particular form of something, such as a program, that is different from earlier forms.
ex: The new version of the app is faster and easier to use.
nat: Make sure you have the latest version before you start the course.

mis.bad: I downloaded the last version of the app.
mis.good: I downloaded the latest version of the app.
mis.why: Use "latest" for the newest version; "last" means final or previous.

def: The name you use to identify yourself when you log in to a system.
ex: You must choose a username that nobody else is already using.
nat: I forgot my username, but I still remember my password.

mis.bad: My user name is wrong, I have not an account.
mis.good: My username is wrong, and I do not have an account.
mis.why: Negation needs the auxiliary: "do not have", not "have not".

def: The physical parts of a computer, such as the screen and the memory.
ex: We need to replace some old hardware before we install the new system.
nat: Hardware problems are often harder to fix than software problems.

mis.bad: We bought three hardwares for the lab.
mis.good: We bought three pieces of hardware for the lab.
mis.why: Hardware is uncountable; use "pieces of hardware" for a number.

def: An organized collection of data stored on a computer so it can be found easily.
ex: All customer details are stored in a database that only managers can access.
nat: The database crashed, and we lost an hour of orders.

mis.bad: I searched in the data bank of the company.
mis.good: I searched the company database.
mis.why: In IT, "banco de dados" is database, not "data bank"; also search takes no preposition.

def: The way a person uses a program or device, including the screens and buttons.
ex: The interface is so simple that even my grandmother can use it.
nat: Users complained that the interface was confusing and full of small buttons.

mis.bad: The program's interface is very bad to use him.
mis.good: The program's interface is very hard to use.
mis.why: After an adjective, the infinitive needs no object pronoun, and "hard to use" is the natural phrase.

def: A person whose job is to create and improve computer programs.
ex: She works as a developer in a company that makes banking apps.
nat: The developers released a patch after users reported the problem.

mis.bad: I am a developer of softwares.
mis.good: I am a software developer.
mis.why: Say "software developer"; software is uncountable and has no plural.

def: A program that talks with people through text or voice, often to answer questions.
ex: The company uses a chatbot to answer simple questions from customers at night.
nat: The chatbot could not understand my question, so I asked for a human.

mis.bad: The chatbot answered me in a very natural form.
mis.good: The chatbot answered me in a very natural way.
mis.why: Use "in a natural way" or "naturally"; "in a natural form" means something different.

def: Space on a device or system where data is kept.
ex: My phone has no storage left, so I can't take any more photos.
nat: The company pays a monthly fee for cloud storage.

mis.bad: My phone has no more space of storage.
mis.good: My phone has no more storage space.
mis.why: Use the noun phrase "storage space" instead of "space of storage".

def: A person who uses computer skills to get into systems without permission.
ex: A hacker stole thousands of passwords from the online store last year.
nat: The bank hired a hacker to test whether its system was safe.

mis.bad: The hackers invaded my account with a invasion.
mis.good: A hacker broke into my account.
mis.why: Use the phrasal verb "break into", not "invade", for getting into an account illegally.

def: The right or ability to use or enter a system, place, or information.
ex: Only authorized staff have access to the customer database and billing records.
nat: I don't have access to that folder, so I can't open the file.

mis.bad: I have access in the system.
mis.good: I have access to the system.
mis.why: Access is followed by "to", not "in".

pt: login, acesso (entrada com usuário e senha)
def: The process or details used to enter a computer system or account.
ex: Enter your login and password on the left side of the screen.
nat: The login failed three times, so the system blocked my account.

mis.bad: I did my login in the site.
mis.good: I logged in to the site.
mis.why: The noun is login, but the verb is two words: log in. Use "logged in".

def: A set of personal details and settings about a user on a website or app.
ex: Please upload a photo and complete your profile before you apply.
nat: Employers often look at your online profile before they call you.

mis.bad: I updated my profile in LinkedIn.
mis.good: I updated my profile on LinkedIn.
mis.why: Use "on" with websites and apps.

def: To change something so that it suits your own needs or tastes.
ex: You can customize the home screen by adding your favorite apps.
nat: Our software lets you customize reports for each department.

mis.bad: I customized my phone for me.
mis.good: I customized my phone.
mis.why: "For me" is unnecessary; customize already means "make it suit me".

def: To turn a computer off and on again so it starts fresh.
ex: If the screen freezes again, reboot the computer and try once more.
nat: I rebooted the router, and the internet came back immediately.

mis.bad: I reinitiated my computer.
mis.good: I rebooted my computer.
mis.why: Use "reboot" or "restart"; "reinitiate" is not used for computers.

def: To stop working suddenly, used for programs and computers.
ex: The app crashed three times while I was filling in the form.
nat: My laptop crashes every time I open that program.

mis.bad: The app is crashing since yesterday.
mis.good: The app has been crashing since yesterday.
mis.why: Use the present perfect continuous with "since".

def: To stop responding, so that nothing on the screen moves.
ex: My laptop froze while I was presenting, which was very embarrassing.
nat: If the video freezes, close the app and open it again.

mis.bad: My computer is frozing.
mis.good: My computer is freezing.
mis.why: Freeze is irregular and drops the e before -ing: freezing.

def: A device that sends internet data between your devices and the network.
ex: I put the router in the living room so the signal reaches every room.
nat: Turn off the router for ten seconds and then turn it on again.

mis.bad: I turned off and on the router.
mis.good: I turned the router off and on.
mis.why: With a noun object, the usual pattern is verb + object + particle: turn the router off.

def: To move old files or messages to a place where they are stored but not used often.
ex: We archive old customer emails after one year to save space on the server.
nat: She archived the project folder and sent it to the manager.

mis.bad: We need to archive this old emails.
mis.good: We need to archive these old emails.
mis.why: Use "these" with plural nouns.

def: To make an exact copy of something.
ex: You can duplicate the slide if you want to keep the original design.
nat: Someone accidentally duplicated the entire spreadsheet instead of moving it.

mis.bad: I made a duplicata of the file.
mis.good: I made a copy of the file.
mis.why: "Duplicata" is not an English noun; say "copy" or "duplicate".

def: To send data from one program to another or save it in a different format.
ex: You can export the data to a spreadsheet and analyze it there.
nat: We exported all customer records before we closed the old system.

mis.bad: I exported the file for PDF.
mis.good: I exported the file as a PDF.
mis.why: Use "as" for the format: export as a PDF.

def: To bring data from another program or file into the one you are using.
ex: I imported the contact list from my old phone into the new one.
nat: The software can import files from most common formats.

mis.bad: I imported the contacts of the old phone to the new.
mis.good: I imported the contacts from my old phone.
mis.why: Use "from" for the source: import from.

def: To prepare a disk or document so it has a particular layout or structure.
ex: You need to format the document so it matches the company style.
nat: He formatted the USB drive and lost all the files on it.

mis.bad: I formated the text.
mis.good: I formatted the text.
mis.why: The verb doubles the final t: formatted.

def: To separate wanted information from unwanted information.
ex: You can filter the results by date to find the newest reports.
nat: The system filters out spam before it reaches your inbox.

mis.bad: I filtered the results by of date.
mis.good: I filtered the results by date.
mis.why: Use "by date" without "of".

def: To arrange items in a particular order.
ex: You can sort the list by name, date, or size.
nat: I sorted the files into folders so I could find them faster.

mis.bad: I ordered the table by the name.
mis.good: I sorted the table by name.
mis.why: In data, "ordenar" is "sort"; "order" means to request or give a command.

def: An important word that you type to search for information.
ex: Type a keyword into the search box and press Enter.
nat: I tried several keywords, but I could not find the article.

mis.bad: I searched the keyword in the Google.
mis.good: I searched for the keyword on Google.
mis.why: Use "search for" something and "on Google", with no "the".

def: A device that detects changes such as heat, light, or movement.
ex: A sensor in the door turns on the light when someone walks in.
nat: The car has a sensor that warns the driver when it is too close to a wall.

mis.bad: The sensors detects the movement.
mis.good: The sensor detects movement.
mis.why: A singular subject takes a verb with -s; a plural subject does not: "sensors detect".

def: A small electronic device that does a useful job.
ex: He loves buying every new gadget as soon as it appears in the shops.
nat: This little gadget can measure how many steps you walk each day.

mis.bad: I like gadgets of technology.
mis.good: I like technology gadgets.
mis.why: Use the compound "technology gadgets" or "tech gadgets" instead of "gadgets of technology".

def: A new idea, method, or product that is different from what existed before.
ex: The company invests a lot of money in innovation to stay ahead.
nat: Smartphones were a major innovation that changed how we communicate.

mis.bad: The innovations is important for companies.
mis.good: Innovation is important for companies.
mis.why: When used as a general idea, innovation is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

def: No longer modern or useful because newer versions exist.
ex: The system is outdated, so it cannot run the latest programs.
nat: Their website looks outdated, and the information is wrong.

mis.bad: My phone is desatualized.
mis.good: My phone is outdated.
mis.why: "Desatualizado" is outdated, with no Portuguese form.

def: Protected against danger, theft, or unauthorized access.
ex: Make sure the connection is secure before you enter your card number.
nat: We store data on a secure server that only a few people can reach.

mis.bad: My password is very safe of hackers.
mis.good: My password is very secure.
mis.why: For passwords and systems, "secure" is the natural word; "safe of" is wrong.

def: Something that could cause damage or harm.
ex: Cyber threats are growing, so every company must protect its data.
nat: The main threat to our system comes from careless employees.

mis.bad: The threat for the system is high.
mis.good: The threat to the system is high.
mis.why: Use "to", not "for", after threat.

def: An attempt to damage or take control of a computer system.
ex: The hospital's network was shut down by a ransomware attack.
nat: Experts say the attack started with a single fake email.

mis.bad: They did an attack in our server.
mis.good: They launched an attack on our server.
mis.why: Use "launch an attack on", not "do an attack in".

def: A small file that a website saves on your device to remember information about you.
ex: The site asked me to accept cookies before it would show the page.
nat: You can delete cookies in your browser settings to protect your privacy.

mis.bad: I accepted the cookie of the site.
mis.good: I accepted the site's cookies.
mis.why: The sites use many cookies, so the plural is needed.

def: A dishonest trick used to take money or information from people.
ex: My grandfather lost money in an online scam that pretended to be a bank.
nat: If an offer sounds too good to be true, it is probably a scam.

mis.bad: I fell in a scam.
mis.good: I fell for a scam.
mis.why: The phrasal expression is "fall for a scam", not "fall in".

def: To check that something is true, correct, or real.
ex: Please verify your email address by clicking the link we sent you.
nat: We verified the numbers twice before sending the report.

mis.bad: Verify the link before click on it.
mis.good: Verify the link before clicking on it.
mis.why: After "before", use the -ing form.

def: To stop someone or something from using or reaching a system.
ex: The firewall blocked the suspicious message before anyone could open it.
nat: I blocked his number because he kept calling me.

mis.bad: The company blocked me of the website.
mis.good: The company blocked my access to the website.
mis.why: Block takes the thing blocked as an object, so say "blocked my access to".

def: A message that warns you about a problem or something important.
ex: The system sent an alert when the server was running out of space.
nat: I received a security alert saying someone had tried to log in.

mis.bad: I received a alert in my phone.
mis.good: I received an alert on my phone.
mis.why: Use "an" before a vowel sound, and "on" for a phone.

def: A file that records what happens in a system, step by step.
ex: The engineer checked the log to find out why the server stopped.
nat: Every user action is saved in the log for later review.

mis.bad: I read the logs of the day to find who deleted.
mis.good: I read the log to find out who deleted the file.
mis.why: To discover information use the phrasal verb "find out".

def: Help given to customers who have problems with a product or service.
ex: I called technical support, and they fixed the problem in ten minutes.
nat: The company offers free support for the first year.

mis.bad: I called the support and he solved it.
mis.good: I called support, and they solved it.
mis.why: In this sense, support has no "the", and a team is referred to as "they".

def: Work done regularly to keep a system or machine in good condition.
ex: The website will be unavailable on Sunday because of scheduled maintenance.
nat: Regular maintenance of the servers prevents serious problems later.

mis.bad: The maintenance of the servers are done weekly.
mis.good: The maintenance of the servers is done weekly.
mis.why: The subject is "maintenance", which is singular.

def: Not likely to change suddenly or stop working.
ex: The new version is more stable and rarely crashes, even with many users.
nat: You need a stable internet connection for a video call.

mis.bad: The connection is more stable of the old one.
mis.good: The connection is more stable than the old one.
mis.why: Use "than" in comparisons, not "of".

def: To make a new product, website, or program available to the public for the first time.
ex: The company launched its new app in March, and it became popular quickly.
nat: They plan to launch the website before the end of the year.

mis.bad: The company lauched the app.
mis.good: The company launched the app.
mis.why: Launch is spelled with "unch" at the end, and the past form adds -ed: launched.

def: To check whether something works correctly or is good enough.
ex: We tested the new feature with real users before the release.
nat: Please test the link before you send it to the clients.

mis.bad: I tested the program with success.
mis.good: I tested the program successfully.
mis.why: Use the adverb "successfully", or say "the test was successful".

def: An online place where people post questions and discuss topics.
ex: I found the solution on a forum for people who repair old computers.
nat: She asked her question in a forum, and three people replied within an hour.

mis.bad: I asked in the forum site.
mis.good: I asked on a forum.
mis.why: Use "on a forum" for online forums.

def: The part of a device that shows information, or the information shown.
ex: The phone has a bright display that is easy to read outdoors.
nat: The display shows the time, the date, and the battery level.

mis.bad: The monitor display have 27 inches.
mis.good: The monitor has a 27-inch display.
mis.why: Use "has" for a singular subject, and describe size with a compound adjective: 27-inch.

def: A set of steps that a computer follows to solve a problem or complete a task.
ex: The search engine uses a complex algorithm to decide which pages appear first.
nat: Social media companies change their algorithms often, so posts reach fewer people.

mis.bad: The algorithm are very complicated.
mis.good: The algorithm is very complicated.
mis.why: Algorithm is singular, so it takes "is".

def: To find and fix mistakes in a computer program.
ex: It took her two days to debug the code and find the real problem.
nat: Developers often debug programs by running them one line at a time.

mis.bad: I debuged the program.
mis.good: I debugged the program.
mis.why: The final g doubles before -ed: debugged.

def: Internet-based servers where data and programs are stored instead of on your own device.
ex: We moved our files to the cloud so every employee can reach them from home.
nat: Your photos are saved in the cloud, so you will not lose them if the phone breaks.

mis.bad: I saved the photos on the cloud.
mis.good: I saved the photos in the cloud.
mis.why: The fixed expression is "in the cloud".

def: To get into a computer system without permission.
ex: Criminals hacked the airline's website and stole the details of many customers.
nat: My social media account was hacked, and someone posted strange messages.

mis.bad: Someone hacked my account and stole me 500 dollars.
mis.good: Someone hacked my account and stole 500 dollars from me.
mis.why: Steal takes the thing as its object; the person comes after "from".

def: A program that finds and removes harmful software from a computer.
ex: The antivirus found a suspicious file and moved it to quarantine.
nat: Make sure your antivirus is up to date before you download anything.

mis.bad: I installed a antivirus.
mis.good: I installed an antivirus program.
mis.why: Use "an" before a vowel sound, and "program" or "software" makes the phrase more natural.

def: To give official permission for someone to do something.
ex: Only the manager can authorize payments above one thousand dollars.
nat: The system will not let you in unless an administrator authorizes your account.

mis.bad: I authorized him to do the purchase.
mis.good: I authorized him to make the purchase.
mis.why: Use "make a purchase", not "do a purchase".

def: Approval that allows someone to do something or use something.
ex: You need permission from the administrator to install new programs.
nat: The app asks for permission to use your camera and microphone.

mis.bad: I need a permission to enter.
mis.good: I need permission to enter.
mis.why: Permission is uncountable here, so do not use "a".

def: Able to work together with another device or program without problems.
ex: This printer is not compatible with the newest version of the system.
nat: Check that the cable is compatible with your phone before you buy it.

mis.bad: This app is compatible to my phone.
mis.good: This app is compatible with my phone.
mis.why: Use "with" after compatible, not "to".

def: A delay between an action and its result, especially online.
ex: The lag during the video call made it hard to have a normal conversation.
nat: There was too much lag in the game, so I stopped playing.

mis.bad: The game has a big delay of lag.
mis.good: The game has a lot of lag.
mis.why: Lag is uncountable here, so say "a lot of lag".

def: To become too hot, usually because a device is working too hard.
ex: My laptop overheats when I run several programs at the same time.
nat: The phone may overheat if you leave it in direct sunlight.

mis.bad: My phone is overheating itself.
mis.good: My phone is overheating.
mis.why: Overheat is intransitive, so it needs no reflexive object.

def: To make data the same on two or more devices or accounts.
ex: The app syncs your notes automatically between your phone and your computer.
nat: I need to sync my calendar with my work email.

mis.bad: I need to sync my phone to the computer.
mis.good: I need to sync my phone with the computer.
mis.why: Use "with" after sync.

def: Damaged so that it cannot be opened or used correctly.
ex: The file was corrupt, so I had to ask her to send it again.
nat: A power cut during the update can leave the system corrupt.

mis.bad: My file is corrupt of the virus.
mis.good: My file was corrupted by a virus.
mis.why: Use the passive "was corrupted by" for the cause.

def: A request for information from a database or a search system.
ex: The query returned thousands of records, so it took a long time to load.
nat: She wrote a query to find all customers who bought something last month.

mis.bad: I did a query in the database.
mis.good: I ran a query on the database.
mis.why: Use "run a query", and "on" the database.

def: The study of data to find patterns that help make decisions.
ex: Our analytics show that most visitors leave the site after ten seconds.
nat: The marketing team uses analytics to understand what customers want.

mis.bad: We need an analytic of the sales.
mis.good: We need an analysis of the sales.
mis.why: "Analytic" is an adjective; the noun for a study is "analysis".

def: A number used to measure how well something is working.
ex: Response time is the most important metric for our support team.
nat: We track several metrics, including cost per customer and monthly sales.

mis.bad: The metrics is improving.
mis.good: The metrics are improving.
mis.why: Metrics is plural, so it takes "are".

def: A screen that shows the most important information in one place.
ex: The manager checks the sales dashboard every morning before the meeting.
nat: The dashboard shows how many tickets are still open.

mis.bad: I looked the dashboard to see the numbers.
mis.good: I looked at the dashboard to see the numbers.
mis.why: Look needs "at" before the thing you are watching.

def: A connection between two things that change together.
ex: There is a strong correlation between hours of sleep and productivity at work.
nat: The data show no correlation between price and customer satisfaction.

mis.bad: There is a correlation of the two.
mis.good: There is a correlation between the two.
mis.why: Use "correlation between" two things.

def: The quality of being correct and without mistakes.
ex: The accuracy of the translation was impressive, even for technical terms.
nat: The model's accuracy improved after we added more training data.

mis.bad: The accuracy of the model is of 95%.
mis.good: The accuracy of the model is 95%.
mis.why: Do not add "of" before the percentage.

def: A computer program or system trained on data to make predictions or decisions.
ex: The team trained a language model on millions of pages of text.
nat: The model works well on common questions but fails on unusual ones.

mis.bad: I created a modelo to the company.
mis.good: I created a model for the company.
mis.why: Use the English word model and "for" the company.

def: The use of machines or software to do work without people.
ex: Automation has replaced many repetitive jobs in factories and offices.
nat: Automation saves us hours of manual work every week.

mis.bad: The automatization of the process saved time.
mis.good: The automation of the process saved time.
mis.why: The English noun is automation, not "automatization".

def: A small flying machine without a pilot, controlled from the ground.
ex: The farmer used a drone to check the crops from above.
nat: Drones are now used to deliver small packages in some cities.

mis.bad: Drones are very useful to take photos.
mis.good: Drones are very useful for taking photos.
mis.why: After "useful", use "for" plus -ing for the purpose.

def: An electronic device, such as a smartwatch, that you wear on your body.
ex: Many runners use a wearable to track their heart rate during training.
nat: New wearables can measure your sleep and warn you about health problems.

mis.bad: I use a wearable to monitor my sleeps.
mis.good: I use a wearable to monitor my sleep.
mis.why: In this sense, sleep is uncountable.

def: No longer used because something newer and better exists.
ex: Floppy disks became obsolete when USB drives and the cloud appeared.
nat: Technology moves so fast that some skills become obsolete in a few years.

mis.bad: This software is obsolete since 2015.
mis.good: This software has been obsolete since 2015.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with "since" for a state that continues until now.

def: Easy to understand and use without needing instructions.
ex: The app is very intuitive, so new users can start using it right away.
nat: An intuitive design means customers do not need to read the manual.

mis.bad: The app is very intuitive to use him.
mis.good: The app is very intuitive to use.
mis.why: Do not add "him" to an infinitive after an adjective.

def: Smooth and continuous, with no breaks or problems.
ex: Customers expect a seamless experience between the website and the mobile app.
nat: The migration was seamless, and nobody noticed any difference.

mis.bad: The integration was seamlessly.
mis.good: The integration was seamless.
mis.why: After "be", use the adjective, not the adverb.

def: Strong and unlikely to fail, even under pressure.
ex: We need a robust system that can handle thousands of users at once.
nat: The company built a robust process to protect customer data.

mis.bad: We need a system robust.
mis.good: We need a robust system.
mis.why: In English the adjective comes before the noun.

def: Easy to attack, damage, or harm.
ex: Old software is more vulnerable to attacks because it lacks security fixes.
nat: The system was vulnerable, so hackers entered within minutes.

mis.bad: The server is vulnerable of attacks.
mis.good: The server is vulnerable to attacks.
mis.why: Use "to" after vulnerable.

def: To use a weakness in a system to get access or cause damage.
ex: Hackers exploited a weakness in the software to steal customer data.
nat: Criminals can exploit old systems that no longer receive updates.

mis.bad: Hackers explored the failure of the system.
mis.good: Hackers exploited a weakness in the system.
mis.why: In security, "explorar uma falha" is exploit, not explore.

def: The act of following the movement or activity of a person or thing.
ex: Many apps use tracking to learn where you go and what you buy.
nat: You can turn off location tracking in your phone settings.

mis.bad: I want the tracking of my package, please say me.
mis.good: I want to track my package, please.
mis.why: Use the verb track, and avoid "say me".

def: Permission that someone gives freely for something to happen.
ex: Websites must ask for your consent before they collect personal data.
nat: She gave her consent for the company to use her photo.

mis.bad: I gave my consentment to the company.
mis.good: I gave my consent to the company.
mis.why: The noun is consent, not "consentment".

def: Without a name, or not showing who you are.
ex: The survey is anonymous, so you can answer every question honestly without worrying.
nat: Someone sent an anonymous email warning us about the problem.

mis.bad: I prefer to stay in anonymous.
mis.good: I prefer to remain anonymous.
mis.why: Anonymous is an adjective, so it takes no "in", and "remain" is the natural verb.

def: Who a person is, or the details that show who they are.
ex: Criminals stole his identity and opened accounts in his name.
nat: You must prove your identity before the bank will change the password.

mis.bad: I lost my identity at the airport.
mis.good: I lost my identity card at the airport.
mis.why: "Identity" means who you are; the physical document is an ID card or identity card.

def: To check or prove that something is correct and acceptable.
ex: The system validates every email address before it saves the new customer account.
nat: Before launch, we validated the results with an independent team.

mis.bad: I validated my ticket in the machine.
mis.good: I validated my ticket at the machine.
mis.why: Use "at" for the location of a machine.

def: To make something visible or available to people who should not see it.
ex: The error exposed the personal details of thousands of customers.
nat: A reporter exposed the problem after reading the leaked documents.

mis.bad: The error exposed the clients' data to the world of internet.
mis.good: The error exposed the clients' data to the public.
mis.why: Use "the public"; "the world of internet" is unnatural.

def: To tell people something that was secret or private.
ex: The company did not disclose how many accounts were affected.
nat: Employees must not disclose confidential information to outsiders.

mis.bad: The company did not disclose to us the numbers of customers.
mis.good: The company did not disclose the number of customers.
mis.why: Disclose takes the information directly as its object, with no "to us" in between.

def: To limit what someone can do or what is allowed.
ex: The company restricts access to the server room to authorized staff.
nat: Some countries restrict the use of certain apps.

mis.bad: I restricted him to enter.
mis.good: I restricted his access.
mis.why: Restrict takes an object that is limited, not an infinitive.

def: To discover or notice something that is hard to see.
ex: The software detected unusual activity on the network last night.
nat: It is difficult to detect errors in such a long document.

mis.bad: The system detected that has a virus.
mis.good: The system detected that there was a virus.
mis.why: The clause needs a subject: "there was a virus".

def: To find the origin of something by following clues or records.
ex: Police traced the attack back to a computer in another country.
nat: Engineers traced the problem to a faulty cable.

mis.bad: The police traced the criminal by the telephone.
mis.good: The police traced the criminal through his phone.
mis.why: Use "through" and a specific item; "by the telephone" is unnatural.

def: A record of a problem or request in a support system.
ex: I opened a ticket, and the support team replied the same day.
nat: The ticket was closed once the issue was fixed.

mis.bad: I opened a call to the support.
mis.good: I opened a ticket with support.
mis.why: In IT, a "chamado" is a ticket; use "with support".

def: The amount that something can hold, handle, or produce.
ex: The server reached its capacity, so new users could not connect.
nat: The stadium has a capacity of fifty thousand people.

mis.bad: The capacity of the disk is of 500 GB.
mis.good: The capacity of the disk is 500 GB.
mis.why: Do not add "of" before the number.

def: The quality of working well and being trustworthy every time.
ex: Customers choose our service because of its reliability and fast support.
nat: The reliability of the network is more important than its speed.

mis.bad: The reliability of the network is of 99%.
mis.good: The reliability of the network is 99%.
mis.why: Do not add "of" before a number.

def: Whether something can be used or reached when needed.
ex: Our main goal is the availability of the service, twenty-four hours a day.
nat: Please check the availability of the room before you book.

mis.bad: The availability of him is low.
mis.good: His availability is low.
mis.why: Use the possessive "his availability".

def: An early model of a product used to test ideas before the final version.
ex: The team built a prototype of the app and tested it with ten users.
nat: The first prototype was too slow, so we redesigned the whole system.

mis.bad: We built a prototype of low cost.
mis.good: We built a low-cost prototype.
mis.why: Use a compound adjective before the noun: low-cost.

def: To create conditions that copy a real situation, usually using a computer.
ex: Engineers simulate heavy traffic to test whether the website can survive.
nat: The software can simulate how a building reacts to an earthquake.

mis.bad: I simulated that I was sick.
mis.good: I pretended to be sick.
mis.why: In English, "simulate" is technical; to pretend an illness, use pretend.

def: A fast internet connection that can send a lot of data.
ex: We finally got broadband in our village, so working from home is possible.
nat: High-speed broadband is now available in most big cities.

mis.bad: I have a large band at home.
mis.good: I have broadband at home.
mis.why: "Banda larga" is broadband, not "large band".

def: A machine sent into space that circles the Earth and sends information.
ex: Weather satellites help scientists predict storms days before they arrive.
nat: The village gets its internet through a satellite because cables do not reach there.

mis.bad: The signal comes by the satellite.
mis.good: The signal comes from a satellite.
mis.why: Use "from" for the source of a signal.

def: To send information or signals from one place to another.
ex: The device transmits data to the server every five minutes.
nat: Radio waves can transmit information over very long distances.

mis.bad: The data was transmitted to the satellite by the signal of radio.
mis.good: The data was transmitted to the satellite by radio signal.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "radio signal".

def: An official right that stops others from making or selling your invention.
ex: The company filed a patent for its new battery technology.
nat: Who owns the patent for this invention?

mis.bad: I registered a patent in my idea.
mis.good: I filed a patent for my idea.
mis.why: Use "file a patent for".

def: The legal right to control who can copy or use a creative work.
ex: You cannot use that photo without permission because it is protected by copyright.
nat: The song is under copyright until the end of the next decade.

mis.bad: The photo has copyrights.
mis.good: The photo is protected by copyright.
mis.why: Copyright is uncountable and is "protected by" it.

def: An official document that gives you permission to use something or do something.
ex: You need a license to use this software on more than one computer.
nat: The company bought a license for fifty employees.

mis.bad: I bought a licence of 50 users.
mis.good: I bought a license for 50 users.
mis.why: Use "for" with the number of users; in US English the noun is spelled license.

def: A level of quality or a rule that is accepted as normal or correct.
ex: The company follows international security standards to protect its data.
nat: This device meets the standard required for use in hospitals.

mis.bad: It is out of the standard.
mis.good: It is not up to standard.
mis.why: The fixed expression is "up to standard".

def: One of the parts that make up a larger system or machine.
ex: Each component of the system is tested separately before final assembly.
nat: A faulty component caused the machine to stop working.

mis.bad: The components of the machine is old.
mis.good: The components of the machine are old.
mis.why: A plural subject takes "are".

def: The basic systems and equipment a company or country needs to work.
ex: The company invested millions in its IT infrastructure last year.
nat: Poor infrastructure makes it hard for businesses to grow in the region.

mis.bad: The infrastructures are old.
mis.good: The infrastructure is old.
mis.why: Infrastructure is uncountable and has no plural.

def: The overall design and structure of a computer system.
ex: The architecture of the system allows it to grow when more users arrive.
nat: Changing the architecture would take months and cost a lot.

mis.bad: He is a software architecture.
mis.good: He is a software architect.
mis.why: The person is an architect; architecture is the field or the design.

def: A short program that automates a simple task.
ex: She wrote a script that renames hundreds of files in a few seconds.
nat: I ran the script, and it fixed the error automatically.

mis.bad: I did a script to rename the files.
mis.good: I wrote a script to rename the files.
mis.why: Use "write a script", not "do a script".

def: An instruction that you type or give to make a computer do something.
ex: Type this command in the terminal and press Enter to start the program.
nat: If the command fails, check that you typed it correctly.

mis.bad: Digit the command and press Enter.
mis.good: Type the command and press Enter.
mis.why: "Digitar" is "type"; "digit" is only a number character.

def: Information or data that is put into a computer or system.
ex: The program rejects any input that contains special characters or is too long.
nat: We value your input, so please tell us what you think of the plan.

mis.bad: I need your inputs about the project.
mis.good: I need your input on the project.
mis.why: Input is uncountable in this sense and takes "on" the topic.

def: The result produced by a computer program or a machine.
ex: Check the output to make sure the program worked correctly.
nat: The factory doubled its output after it bought new machines.

mis.bad: The outputs of the program is wrong.
mis.good: The program's output is wrong.
mis.why: Use a singular verb with a singular subject, and the possessive reads more naturally.

def: A value or limit that you set to control how a system works.
ex: You can change the parameters to make the program run faster.
nat: The report was created within strict parameters set by the manager.

mis.bad: Parameters is set by the user.
mis.good: Parameters are set by the user.
mis.why: Plural subjects need "are".

def: To run a program or carry out an instruction.
ex: The program executes the commands in the order they are written.
nat: The system executed the task automatically at midnight.

mis.bad: I executed the program with success.
mis.good: I ran the program successfully.
mis.why: Use "successfully", and "run" sounds more natural for a program.

def: A place that stores data temporarily so it can be loaded faster.
ex: Clear your browser cache if the page does not update.
nat: The app saves images in the cache so that they appear quickly.

mis.bad: I cleaned the cache of the browser.
mis.good: I cleared the browser cache.
mis.why: Say "clear the cache"; "clean" is for physical dirt.

def: The part of a computer that holds data or programs for use.
ex: The program uses too much memory, so the computer becomes slow.
nat: This laptop has sixteen gigabytes of memory.

mis.bad: My computer has little memory of storage.
mis.good: My computer has little memory.
mis.why: Use "memory" for RAM, and skip "of storage", which is a different concept.

def: The part of a computer that carries out instructions and calculations.
ex: The new processor makes the laptop twice as fast as the old one.
nat: A slow processor can ruin the experience of playing modern games.

mis.bad: This processor is more fast than the old one.
mis.good: This processor is faster than the old one.
mis.why: Short adjectives take -er, not "more".

def: To make a file smaller so that it uses less space.
ex: You should compress the photos before you send them by email.
nat: The program compresses videos without a noticeable loss of quality.

mis.bad: I compressed the file in a zip of 5MB.
mis.good: I compressed the file to 5 MB.
mis.why: Use "to" for the final size.

def: To take out data or files from a larger source or archive.
ex: The tool extracts the text from PDF files and saves it in a document.
nat: You must extract the files from the zip folder before you can open them.

mis.bad: I extracted the files of the folder.
mis.good: I extracted the files from the folder.
mis.why: Use "from" for the source: extract from.

def: To move data or files from one place to another.
ex: I transferred all my photos from my old phone to my laptop.
nat: The bank will transfer the money to your account tomorrow.

mis.bad: I transfered the files to the new computer.
mis.good: I transferred the files to the new computer.
mis.why: The final r doubles before -ed: transferred.

def: Careful watching of people or places, especially by cameras or software.
ex: Cameras in the street have increased public surveillance in many cities.
nat: Many people worry about government surveillance of online activity.

mis.bad: The company is under surveillance of the police.
mis.good: The company is under police surveillance.
mis.why: Use "under police surveillance" as a fixed phrase.

def: To protect something from harm or loss.
ex: The company introduced strict new rules to safeguard customer information from online criminals.
nat: Strong passwords help safeguard your accounts against theft.

mis.bad: We safeguard the customers of the data.
mis.good: We safeguard customer data.
mis.why: Say "customer data"; the sentence needed no "of the".

def: A set of rules that explain how to do something or how devices communicate.
ex: All staff must follow the security protocol when they leave the building.
nat: The two systems communicate using a standard network protocol.

mis.bad: Give me the protocol of the request.
mis.good: Give me the reference number for the request.
mis.why: In English, "protocol" is a set of rules, not a receipt number.

def: Something that is different from what is normal or expected.
ex: The system raised an alert when it noticed an anomaly in the data.
nat: There is an anomaly in the sales figures for March.

mis.bad: I saw an anormality in the data.
mis.good: I saw an anomaly in the data.
mis.why: The English noun is anomaly; "anormality" is not used.

def: Harmful software that locks a user's files until they pay money.
ex: The hospital had to cancel operations after a ransomware attack.
nat: Regular backups can protect you from ransomware.

mis.bad: Ransomwares are dangerous.
mis.good: Ransomware is dangerous.
mis.why: Ransomware is uncountable and has no plural.

def: An unwanted entry into a system, place, or private matter.
ex: The company installed a system to detect any network intrusion.
nat: She felt the constant messages were an intrusion into her private life.

mis.bad: The intrusion in our server was found.
mis.good: The intrusion into our server was found.
mis.why: Use "into" after intrusion.

def: The amount of time a system is working and available.
ex: Our hosting provider promises ninety-nine percent uptime, which is important for online shops.
nat: High uptime is critical for online shops, especially during sales.

mis.bad: The uptime of the site was down.
mis.good: The site was down for an hour.
mis.why: Uptime is the time a system works; use "down" for an outage.

def: To repeat a process many times, making improvements each time.
ex: The team iterated on the design until users were happy with it.
nat: We iterate quickly, releasing small updates every week.

mis.bad: We iterated the design to more times.
mis.good: We iterated on the design twice.
mis.why: Use "iterate on" a design, and "twice" for number of times.

def: To change information into a digital form that a computer can use.
ex: The library is digitizing thousands of old books so people can read them online.
nat: We digitized our paper records last year to save space.

mis.bad: We digitalized the documents of the company.
mis.good: We digitized the company's documents.
mis.why: The verb is digitize; "digitalize" is rare and means something broader.

def: To interrupt something or change it greatly, especially by new technology.
ex: New apps have disrupted the taxi industry in many countries.
nat: A power cut disrupted the service for several hours.

mis.bad: The storm disrupted the traffic of the city.
mis.good: The storm disrupted traffic in the city.
mis.why: Traffic is uncountable, and "in the city" is the natural phrase.

def: Describes software whose code can be seen, used, and changed by anyone.
ex: They chose an open-source tool because it was free and flexible.
nat: Many open-source projects depend on volunteers who work in their free time.

mis.bad: The software is open source code.
mis.good: The software is open source.
mis.why: As a predicate, the phrase is written "open source" without the word "code".

def: Owned by a company and not free for others to use or copy.
ex: The company uses proprietary software that only its own staff can modify.
nat: Proprietary technology gives a company an advantage over its competitors.

mis.bad: It is a software proprietary of the company.
mis.good: It is proprietary software owned by the company.
mis.why: The adjective goes before the noun, and "owned by" shows ownership.

def: A detailed description of what something must be or do.
ex: The engineers checked the product against the specification before delivery.
nat: Please read the technical specifications before you order the part.

mis.bad: The client changed the specification in the last minute.
mis.good: The client changed the specification at the last minute.
mis.why: The fixed expression is "at the last minute".

def: A temporary space in memory where data waits before it is used.
ex: The video stopped because the buffer ran out of data.
nat: A larger buffer can reduce delays when you stream music.

mis.bad: The video is buffering of the internet.
mis.good: The video is buffering because of the internet.
mis.why: Use "because of" to give a reason.

def: To find a way around a rule, system, or problem.
ex: Some users try to circumvent the filter by using a different network.
nat: The company found a clever way to circumvent the legal problem.

mis.bad: I circumvented around the filter.
mis.good: I circumvented the filter.
mis.why: Circumvent is a transitive verb and takes no "around".

def: To change something without permission, often in order to damage it.
ex: Someone tampered with the security camera a few minutes before the robbery happened.
nat: The seal shows if anyone has tampered with the package.

mis.bad: Someone tampered the lock.
mis.good: Someone tampered with the lock.
mis.why: Tamper is always followed by "with".

def: To fake the source of an email or call so it looks real.
ex: Criminals spoofed the bank's number, so the call looked genuine.
nat: Attackers often spoof email addresses to trick people into clicking links.

mis.bad: The email was spoof.
mis.good: The email was spoofed.
mis.why: Use the past participle as an adjective: spoofed.

def: To combine many separate pieces of information into one whole.
ex: The dashboard aggregates data from all our offices into one report.
nat: We aggregated the results from several surveys to see the overall trend.

mis.bad: I aggregated the new information to the report.
mis.good: I added the new information to the report.
mis.why: "Agregar" often means "add"; in English use add, since aggregate means combine many items.

def: To remove personal details from data so people cannot be identified.
ex: The researchers anonymized all the data before they published the results online.
nat: Companies must anonymize customer records before they share them.

mis.bad: We anonymized the data for don't identify people.
mis.good: We anonymized the data so that people cannot be identified.
mis.why: "For" cannot be followed by a negative verb; use "so that" plus a clause.

def: To reach a conclusion from evidence rather than direct information.
ex: The model can infer the topic of a text from a few words.
nat: From his tone, I inferred that he was not happy with the result.

mis.bad: What are you inferring with that?
mis.good: What are you implying with that?
mis.why: Infer means to conclude; implying is what the speaker does.

def: Able to work or act independently, without direct human control.
ex: Several companies are testing autonomous cars on public roads in different big cities.
nat: The robot is autonomous, so it can find its way around the warehouse.

mis.bad: The car is autonomic.
mis.good: The car is autonomous.
mis.why: "Autonomic" refers to body functions; for machines use autonomous.

def: Seeming to be present everywhere at the same time.
ex: Smartphones have become ubiquitous, and nearly everyone carries one in their pocket.
nat: Wi-Fi is now ubiquitous in cafes, hotels, and airports.

mis.bad: The phones are ubiquitous in everywhere.
mis.good: Phones are ubiquitous.
mis.why: Ubiquitous already means "everywhere", so do not add it again.

def: A place where data, files, or code is stored and managed.
ex: All our code is stored in a central repository that everyone can access.
nat: She uploaded the latest changes to the repository this morning.

mis.bad: I pushed the code in the repository.
mis.good: I pushed the code to the repository.
mis.why: Use "to" for the destination of a push.

def: The process of changing data into a secret code so that only authorized people can read it.
ex: Strong encryption keeps your messages private even if someone intercepts them on the network.
nat: The app uses end-to-end encryption, so even the company cannot read your chats.

mis.bad: We use cryptography on the files to protect them.
mis.good: We use encryption to protect the files.
mis.why: As a security tool, "criptografia" is encryption; cryptography is the science behind it.

def: The process of proving that you are who you say you are.
ex: The bank added two-factor authentication to make stolen passwords less useful to criminals.
nat: Authentication failed because I typed the wrong code from my phone.

mis.bad: The authentication was failed.
mis.good: Authentication failed.
mis.why: Fail is intransitive, so it cannot be used in the passive voice.

def: The ability of a system to handle more work or users as it grows.
ex: Scalability is the main reason the company chose cloud servers instead of its own.
nat: Before we launch, we must test the scalability of the system.

mis.bad: The system has a good scalability.
mis.good: The system has good scalability.
mis.why: Scalability is uncountable here, so it does not take "a".

def: A small program that adds a new feature to a larger program.
ex: I installed a plugin that blocks ads and stops websites from tracking me.
nat: The browser supports hundreds of plugins made by independent developers.

mis.bad: This plugin permits to edit videos.
mis.good: This plugin lets you edit videos.
mis.why: Permit is not followed directly by an infinitive; use "let someone do" or "allow someone to do".

def: To switch a setting on or off, or to move between two options.
ex: You can toggle dark mode on and off from the settings menu.
nat: She toggled between two windows while she wrote the report.

mis.bad: I toggled the setting of on to off.
mis.good: I toggled the setting from on to off.
mis.why: Use "from ... to" to show the change.

def: Using body features such as fingerprints or the face to identify a person.
ex: Many phones now use biometric data, such as a fingerprint, to unlock the screen.
nat: Airports are introducing biometric checks to speed up passport control.

mis.bad: The phone has biometry.
mis.good: The phone has biometric authentication.
mis.why: In everyday English use the adjective biometric, as in biometric data; "biometry" is not used for this.

def: Data that describes other data, such as the date and author of a file.
ex: The photo's metadata shows the date, the time, and the place it was taken.
nat: Journalists checked the metadata to confirm when the document was created.

mis.bad: The metadatas are hidden.
mis.good: The metadata is hidden.
mis.why: Metadata is uncountable, so it has no plural -s.

def: Something that a program or system needs in order to work, or a strong need for something.
ex: The update failed because one dependency was missing from the server.
nat: Our dependency on one supplier became a serious risk for the business.

mis.bad: Our dependency of one supplier is a risk.
mis.good: Our dependency on one supplier is a risk.
mis.why: Use "on" after dependency.

def: Permanent software built into a device that controls how its hardware works.
ex: The camera stopped working after I installed the wrong firmware version.
nat: Manufacturers release a firmware update to fix security problems in routers.

mis.bad: I need to update the firmwares of my router.
mis.good: I need to update the firmware on my router.
mis.why: Firmware is uncountable, like software.

def: A record of the exact date and time when something happened.
ex: Each message in the log has a timestamp, so we can see the order.
nat: The investigator compared the timestamps of the two files to find the original.

mis.bad: The log has a stamp of time for each event.
mis.good: The log has a timestamp for each event.
mis.why: Use the single word timestamp; "stamp of time" is not used.

def: A device connected to a network, or a point where a program connects to a service.
ex: Security teams must protect every endpoint, including laptops and phones used from home.
nat: The app sends a request to the server's endpoint every few seconds.

mis.bad: We need to protect all the endpoint.
mis.good: We need to protect all the endpoints.
mis.why: Each device is a separate endpoint, so use the plural after "all the".

def: A safe, separate environment where you can test programs without harming the real system.
ex: We ran the suspicious file in a sandbox to see what it would do.
nat: Developers test new features in a sandbox before releasing them to customers.

mis.bad: We tested the program at the sandbox.
mis.good: We tested the program in a sandbox.
mis.why: Use "in" for a sandbox environment.

def: A fake video or audio made with AI to look or sound like a real person.
ex: The video was a deepfake, but it looked so real that many people believed it.
nat: Experts warn that deepfakes can be used to spread false news before elections.

mis.bad: He was victim of a deepfake.
mis.good: He was the victim of a deepfake.
mis.why: Use the article "the" before victim.

def: A mobile phone that can also run apps and connect to the internet.
ex: She uses her smartphone to pay bills, book taxis, and check her email.
nat: My smartphone has a great camera, but the battery doesn't last long.

mis.bad: I bought a smartphone of 128 gigabytes.
mis.good: I bought a 128-gigabyte smartphone.
mis.why: Use a compound adjective before the noun, with no plural: 128-gigabyte.

def: A small computer that you can carry and use on a table or on your lap.
ex: I always carry my laptop in my backpack when I travel for work.
nat: The company gave every new employee a laptop and a headset.

mis.bad: I bought a new notebook to study and work.
mis.good: I bought a new laptop to study and work.
mis.why: In English a notebook is usually a paper book; for the computer say laptop.

def: A saved link that lets you return quickly to a web page.
ex: I added the tutorial to my bookmarks so I can find it again later.
nat: She keeps a folder of bookmarks for useful sites about grammar.

mis.bad: I put the page on my favorite.
mis.good: I added the page to my bookmarks.
mis.why: Use bookmark(s) for saved web pages; "favorite" alone is an adjective.

def: A ready-made document or design that you can copy and change.
ex: I used a template to create my résumé, so it took only ten minutes.
nat: The company has a template for every kind of business email.

mis.bad: I used a model of résumé from the internet.
mis.good: I used a résumé template from the internet.
mis.why: A ready-made document to copy is a template; "model" means a person who shows clothes or a simulation.

def: A computer document with rows and columns used to organize and calculate numbers.
ex: She keeps all her expenses in a spreadsheet and checks it every Sunday.
nat: Can you send me the spreadsheet with the sales figures from last quarter?

mis.bad: I made a spreadsheet on Excel.
mis.good: I made a spreadsheet in Excel.
mis.why: Use "in" with Excel and other programs.

def: A small window or message that suddenly appears on your screen.
ex: A pop-up appeared and asked me to accept cookies before I could read.
nat: I installed an extension that blocks every pop-up on the websites I visit.

mis.bad: A pop up appear when I open the site.
mis.good: A pop-up appears when I open the site.
mis.why: Write pop-up with a hyphen, and the verb needs -s after a singular noun.

def: A small camera connected to a computer that is used for video calls.
ex: My webcam stopped working just before the interview, so I used my phone.
nat: Please turn on your webcam so we can see each other during the meeting.

mis.bad: My web cam are not working.
mis.good: My webcam is not working.
mis.why: Webcam is one word, and a singular noun takes "is".

def: A place or a phone feature that gives you wireless internet.
ex: My phone can create a hotspot, so I can work on the train.
nat: The café is a free Wi-Fi hotspot, so it is always full of students.

mis.bad: I shared my internet by the hotspot of the phone.
mis.good: I shared my internet through my phone's hotspot.
mis.why: Use "through" for the means of sharing, with the possessive.

def: A device that gives power to a phone or laptop battery.
ex: I left my charger at the hotel, so I had to buy a new one.
nat: This fast charger can fill the battery in less than an hour.

mis.bad: I need a charger of cellphone.
mis.good: I need a phone charger.
mis.why: Use a noun before the main noun: phone charger.

def: The protection of computers, networks, and data from attacks.
ex: The company hired a new manager to improve cybersecurity across all departments.
nat: Good cybersecurity starts with simple habits, such as using strong passwords.

mis.bad: The cybersecurities of the company are weak.
mis.good: The company's cybersecurity is weak.
mis.why: Cybersecurity is uncountable and has no plural.

def: The use of data to find where a person or device is in the world.
ex: The app uses geolocation to show restaurants that are close to you.
nat: You can disable geolocation in your settings if you do not want to be tracked.

mis.bad: The app asks my geolocalization.
mis.good: The app asks for my location.
mis.why: The English term is geolocation or location, and "ask" needs "for".

def: The act of changing a service so that it suits each user.
ex: Personalization helps online stores show products that each customer is likely to buy.
nat: Some users like personalization, while others worry about how their data is used.

mis.bad: The app has many personalizations options.
mis.good: The app has many personalization options.
mis.why: A noun used as a modifier stays singular: personalization options.

def: A test on a website that checks whether you are a real person and not a robot.
ex: I had to solve a captcha before the website would let me log in.
nat: The captcha showed blurry pictures, and I could not tell which ones had traffic lights.

mis.bad: I need to resolve the captcha.
mis.good: I need to solve the captcha.
mis.why: "Resolver" is "solve" for puzzles; "resolve" means to settle a problem or decide.

def: An attempt to steal, damage, or block data or systems using the internet.
ex: The city's computers stopped working after a cyberattack on Monday morning.
nat: Small businesses are often hit by a cyberattack because their security is weak.

mis.bad: The company suffered an attack cybernetic.
mis.good: The company suffered a cyberattack.
mis.why: "Cibernético" is not "cybernetic" here; use the word cyberattack.

def: Crime that is committed using computers or the internet.
ex: Cybercrime costs businesses billions of dollars every year around the world.
nat: The police created a special unit to investigate cybercrime in the region.

mis.bad: Cybercrimes is increasing every year.
mis.good: Cybercrime is increasing every year.
mis.why: As a general idea, cybercrime is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb.
